<blockquote class="blockquote">

<p class="small font-italic">

There are far more ordinary people (say, 80 percent) than extraordinary people
(say, 20 percent), and this is often characterized by the 80/20 principle, based
on the observation made by the Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto in 1906 that
80% of land in Italy was owned by 20% of the population. A histogram of the data
values for these phenomena would reveal a right-skewed or heavy-tailed
distribution. How to map the data with the heavy-tailed distribution?

</p>

<footer class="blockquote-footer text-right">

Jiang (2013)

</footer>

</blockquote>

## Abstract

This article explains how `classIntervals()` in **classInt** implements
head/tail breaks (Jiang, 2013). A worked example follows the algorithm one
iteration at a time. The case study compares head/tail breaks, Fisher–Jenks
and quantiles using the African conflict data in `spData::afcon`.

## Introduction

**Head/tail breaks** is a classification scheme introduced by Jiang (2013) for
revealing hierarchies in data with many small values and a few large ones. The
related **ht-index** summarizes how deeply this pattern recurs across scales
(Jiang & Yin, 2014).

In the examples below, the distributions are strongly right-skewed. A few
large values form the head and many smaller values form the tail.

Power-law and lognormal distributions are examples of heavy-tailed
distributions. The head/tail breaks literature also uses exponential
distributions to illustrate the imbalance. Rare, large outcomes matter in
applications such as portfolio credit risk (Vasicek, 2002) and in broader
discussions of extreme events (Taleb, 2008).

```{r}
#| label: 20200405_charheavytail
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig-alt:
#|   - Cumulative share of a simulated Pareto sample, ordered from largest to
#|     smallest. The top 20% of observations accounts for about 74% of
#|     the total, below the theoretical 80% reference line.
#|   - Histogram of 1,000 simulated Pareto observations. Most values cluster
#|     near the lower end of the scale, while a long right tail extends beyond
#|     500.

library(classInt)
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)

# Define a common theme for the plots.
background <- "#FEFDFD"

map_title <- "inter-tight"
map_regular <- "inter"

sysfonts::font_add_google("Inter Tight", family = map_title)
sysfonts::font_add_google("Inter", family = map_regular)
showtext::showtext_opts(dpi = knitr::opts_chunk$get("dpi"))
showtext::showtext_auto()

theme_set(
  theme_bw(paper = background, base_family = map_regular) +
    theme(
      rect = element_rect(fill = background),
      plot.title = element_text(family = map_title, face = "bold"),
      legend.title = element_text(family = map_title, face = "bold"),
      strip.text = element_text(family = map_title, face = "bold"),
      plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10)
    )
)

# 1. Characterization of heavy-tail distributions----
set.seed(1234)
# Pareto distribution a=1 b=1.161 n=1000
sample_par <- (1 - runif(1000))^(-1 / (log(5) / log(4)))

sample_par_df <- tibble(x = sample_par) |>
  arrange(desc(x)) |>
  mutate(
    prop = row_number() / n(),
    cumulative = cumsum(x) / sum(x)
  )

ggplot(sample_par_df, aes(prop, cumulative)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.8, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_percent()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent()) +
  labs(
    title = "How much of the total does the top 20% account for?",
    subtitle = "Cumulative share in a simulated Pareto sample",
    x = "Top proportion of observations",
    y = "Cumulative share of total"
  )

# Histogram
ggplot(sample_par_df, aes(x = x)) +
  geom_histogram(
    aes(y = after_stat(density)),
    bins = 100,
    fill = "grey50",
    color = NA
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "A simulated Pareto sample",
    subtitle = "Most observations are small, with a few large values",
    x = "Value",
    y = "Density"
  )
```

## Breaking method

The method itself consists of a four-step process performed recursively until a
stopping condition is satisfied. Given a vector of values $$v = (a_1, a_2,
..., a_n) $$, the process can be described as follows:

1.  Compute the arithmetic mean, $$\mu = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i$$.
2.  Break $$v$$ into the $$tail$$ and the $$head$$:
    $$tail = \{ a_x \in v | a_x \le \mu \} $$
    $$head = \{ a_x \in v | a_x \gt \mu \} $$.
3.  Check whether the proportion of observations in the head is at most the
    chosen threshold: $$\frac{|head|}{|v|} \le threshold  $$
4.  If step 3 is `TRUE` and the head contains at least two observations, replace
    $$v$$ with $$head$$ and repeat. Otherwise, stop.

Only values strictly above the mean enter the next iteration. Values equal to
the mean stay in the tail.

A threshold of 40% is a practical stopping rule (Jiang et al., 2013).
It does not provide a statistical test for a heavy-tailed distribution.

At each iteration, the arithmetic mean separates the head from the tail.
Repeat with the head only if it contains at least two observations and its
share of the sample is at or below the threshold.

{% raw %}
``` mermaid

flowchart TD
    accTitle: Head/tail breaks algorithm
    accDescr: Compute the mean and keep values above it as the head. Repeat with the head only when it has at least two values and its share is at or below the threshold. Keep each mean as a break.
    A["Sample vector&nbsp;$$v = (a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n)$$"]
    B["Compute arithmetic mean&nbsp;$$\mu = \frac{1}{n}\sum a_i$$"]
    C{"Is&nbsp;$$a_i > \mu$$?"}
    D["Tail"]
    E["Head"]
    F{"Is&nbsp;$$\frac{|\text{head}|}{|v|} \le \text{threshold}$$?"}
    G(("Stop"))
    H["Replace sample&nbsp;$$v \leftarrow \text{head}$$"]
    I{"At least two values<br/>in the head?"}

    A --> B
    B --> C

    C -- FALSE --> D
    C -- TRUE --> E

    E --> F

    F -- FALSE --> G
    F -- TRUE --> I
    I -- FALSE --> G
    I -- TRUE --> H

    H -.-> B
```
{% endraw %}

Each iteration produces a new break at the arithmetic mean of the current
sample. Once the stopping condition is met, the final set of breaks is obtained
by collecting the successive means computed throughout the process:

$$ breaks = (\mu_1, \mu_2, \mu_3, ..., \mu_k ) $$

## Step-by-step example

Jiang (2019) summarizes the original procedure in this pseudocode[^1]:

```
Recursive function Head/tail Breaks:
 Rank the input data from the largest to the smallest
 Break the data into the head and the tail around the mean;
 // the head for those above the mean
 // the tail for those below the mean
 While (head <= 40%):
 Head/tail Breaks (head);
End Function
```

The **R** example continues only when `prop < thr`. The pseudocode allows
equality, so the two stop at different points if the head contains exactly
40% of the observations. That case does not occur in this sample.

```{r}
#| label: 20200405_stepbystep
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Four histograms showing successive head/tail breaks iterations. The
#|   shaded area marks the head and the dashed line marks the mean. The share
#|   above the mean is 14.5%, 21.4%, 19.4% and 50%, respectively.

var <- sample_par
thr <- 0.4
brks <- range(var, na.rm = TRUE)

iterations <- list()
summary_rows <- list()

for (i in seq_len(10)) {
  mu <- mean(var)
  head_values <- var[var > mu]
  prop <- length(head_values) / length(var)

  brks <- sort(c(brks, mu))

  iterations[[i]] <- tibble(
    iter = i,
    value = var,
    mu = mu,
    prop = prop
  )

  summary_rows[[i]] <- tibble(
    iter = i,
    mu = mu,
    prop = prop,
    n_var = length(var),
    n_head = length(head_values)
  )

  if (!(prop < thr && length(head_values) > 1)) {
    break
  }

  var <- head_values
}

iter_df <- bind_rows(iterations) |>
  mutate(iter = factor(iter, levels = unique(iter)))

sum_table <- bind_rows(summary_rows)

# Prepare plot
labels_df <- sum_table |>
  mutate(
    iter = factor(iter, levels = levels(iter_df$iter)),
    label = paste0(
      "Share of observations\nin the head:\n",
      label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)(prop)
    )
  )

iter_df |>
  group_by(iter) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(
    bins = 50,
    fill = "grey50",
    color = NA
  ) +
  # Areas
  geom_rect(
    aes(xmin = mu, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
    fill = "red",
    alpha = 0.1,
    data = ~ slice_head(.x, n = 1)
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    data = labels_df,
    aes(xintercept = mu),
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "red3"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = labels_df,
    aes(x = mu, y = Inf, label = label),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    position = position_nudge(x = 20),
    hjust = 0,
    vjust = 1.5,
    size = 3
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    vars(iter),
    scales = "free_y",
    labeller = labeller(iter = ~ paste("Iteration", .x))
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_comma(accuracy = 1),
    breaks = breaks_extended(n = 3)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Head/tail breaks across four iterations",
    subtitle = "Shading marks the head above the mean",
    x = "Value",
    y = "Count"
  )
```

The head accounts for 50% of the remaining observations in the fourth
iteration. That exceeds the 40% threshold and stops the loop.

```{r}
#| label: hiddtable
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: ""
# Summary table
sum_table |>
  mutate(
    mu = round(mu, 4),
    prop = paste0(round(100 * prop, 2), "%")
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)
```

The break vector includes the original minimum and maximum, plus the means
computed during the iterations. Here the original data are `sample_par`, since
`var` is replaced by the head inside the loop.

## Implementation in the **classInt** package

The implementation in `classIntervals()` reproduces these results:

```{r}
#| label: checkmethod
#| fig-cap: ""
# Compare with classInt
ht_sample_par <- classIntervals(
  sample_par,
  style = "headtails"
)

all.equal(brks, ht_sample_par$brks)
```

The data determine the number of breaks (Jiang, 2013). The `thr` argument
controls how large the head can be before recursion stops. In the next figure,
higher thresholds let the algorithm continue for more iterations.

```{r}
#| label: 20200405_examplesimp
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Four panels compare head/tail breaks thresholds of 0, 0.2, 0.4 and 1
#|   against the empirical cumulative distribution of a Pareto sample. Higher
#|   thresholds produce more classes, with boundaries concentrated near the
#|   lower values.

thresholds <- c(0, 0.2, 0.4, 1)

breaks_df <- lapply(thresholds, function(thr) {
  ci <- classIntervals(
    sample_par,
    style = "headtails",
    thr = thr
  )

  tibble(
    threshold = paste0("thr = ", thr),
    value = sample_par,
    class = findInterval(
      sample_par,
      ci$brks,
      all.inside = TRUE
    ),
    n_classes = length(ci$brks) - 1
  ) |>
    # Prepare rect
    group_by(threshold, n_classes, class) |>
    summarise(xmin = min(value), xmax = max(value), .groups = "drop_last") |>
    mutate(
      xmin = ifelse(row_number() == 1, -Inf, lag(xmax)),
      xmax = ifelse(row_number() == n(), Inf, xmax)
    ) |>
    ungroup()
}) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  mutate(
    threshold = factor(
      threshold,
      levels = paste0("thr = ", thresholds)
    )
  )

# Number of classes
breaks_df |>
  distinct(threshold, n_classes) |>
  knitr::kable(row.names = FALSE)

# Distribution of observations across classes
ggplot(breaks_df, aes(fill = factor(class))) +
  stat_ecdf(
    data = tibble(x = sample_par),
    aes(x = x),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  stat_ecdf(
    data = tibble(x = sample_par),
    aes(x = x),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    geom = "point",
    size = 1.5,
    pad = FALSE
  ) +
  # Areas
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf)) +
  facet_wrap(~threshold, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent()) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "cividis", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    title = "How the stopping threshold affects the breaks",
    subtitle = "Four thresholds applied to the same Pareto sample",
    x = "Value",
    y = "Cumulative proportion",
    fill = "Class"
  )
```

Even at `thr = 0`, the algorithm makes the initial split at the mean.
Together with the minimum and maximum, this gives two classes.

## Case study

Jiang (2013) proposed head/tail breaks as a way to reveal the hierarchy in
heavy-tailed data. Here we compare `headtails`, `fisher` (Fisher–Jenks) and
`quantile` using `afcon` from **spData**. Each method uses the same number
of classes as head/tail breaks.

```{r}
#| label: 20200405_loadspdata
#| message: false
#| fig-cap: ""
library(spData)
data(afcon, package = "spData")
```

The variable `totcon` is an index of total conflict from 1966 to 1978.
The table shows the 10 highest values.

```{r}
#| label: 20200405_summspdata
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-alt:
#|   - Histogram of conflict index values for African countries, 1966–1978.
#|     Most countries have low index values. A few exceed 3,000, and the
#|     highest value is about 5,200.
#|   - Estimated density of the conflict index for African countries,
#|     1966–1978. The curve peaks below 1,000 and extends beyond 5,000.
# Top10
knitr::kable(head(
  afcon[order(afcon$totcon, decreasing = TRUE), c("name", "totcon")],
  10
))

ggplot(afcon, aes(x = totcon)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of the conflict index, 1966–1978",
    subtitle = "African countries grouped by index value",
    x = "Conflict index",
    y = "Number of countries",
    caption = "Data source: Anselin & O'Loughlin (1992)"
  )

ggplot(afcon, aes(x = totcon)) +
  geom_density() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  labs(
    title = "The conflict index is right-skewed",
    subtitle = "Density estimate for African countries, 1966–1978",
    x = "Conflict index",
    y = "Density",
    caption = "Data source: Anselin & O'Loughlin (1992)"
  )
```

Egypt and Sudan have the two highest index values. The histogram shows the
same imbalance seen in the simulated sample: many lower values and a few
much larger ones.

Quantile breaks use ranks to put roughly the same number of observations in
each class. The code below applies all three methods to the same data.

```{r}
#| label: 20200405_breaksample
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Three panels compare head/tail breaks, Fisher–Jenks and quantile
#|   classifications of African conflict index values. Colored bands mark five classes
#|   over the empirical cumulative distribution, showing how the methods place
#|   boundaries at different values.

afcon$headtails <- classify_intervals(afcon$totcon, style = "headtails")
afcon$headtails_br <- as.numeric(afcon$headtails)

# Record the number of classes to set the same

nclass <- length(levels(afcon$headtails))

# Same number of classes for "fisher"
afcon$fisher <- classify_intervals(afcon$totcon, style = "fisher", n = nclass)
afcon$fisher_br <- as.numeric(afcon$fisher)

afcon$quantile <- classify_intervals(
  afcon$totcon,
  style = "quantile",
  n = nclass
)
afcon$quantile_br <- as.numeric(afcon$quantile)

levels(afcon$headtails)
levels(afcon$fisher)
levels(afcon$quantile)

ht_breaks <- classIntervals(afcon$totcon, style = "headtails")$brks[seq_len(
  nclass
)]

fisher_breaks <- classIntervals(
  afcon$totcon,
  style = "fisher",
  n = nclass
)$brks[seq_len(nclass)]

q_breaks <- classIntervals(
  afcon$totcon,
  style = "quantile",
  n = nclass
)$brks[seq_len(nclass)]

tibble(
  id_breaks = "Head/tail breaks",
  b = ht_breaks,
  group = as.factor(seq_along(ht_breaks))
) |>
  bind_rows(
    tibble(
      id_breaks = "Fisher–Jenks",
      b = fisher_breaks,
      group = as.factor(seq_along(fisher_breaks))
    )
  ) |>
  bind_rows(
    tibble(
      id_breaks = "Quantiles",
      b = q_breaks,
      group = as.factor(seq_along(q_breaks))
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(id_breaks = fct_inorder(id_breaks)) |>
  # Prepare rects
  group_by(id_breaks) |>
  mutate(
    xmin = if_else(row_number() == 1, -Inf, b),
    xmax = if_else(row_number() == n(), Inf, lead(b))
  ) |>
  ggplot() +
  stat_ecdf(
    data = afcon,
    aes(x = totcon),
    geom = "point",
    size = 1,
    pad = FALSE
  ) +
  # Areas
  geom_rect(aes(
    xmin = xmin, xmax = xmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
    fill = group
  )) +
  facet_wrap(vars(id_breaks), ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent()) +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "cividis", alpha = 0.5) +
  guides(color = guide_legend(), fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(alpha = 1))) +
  labs(
    title = "Where the three methods place their class breaks",
    subtitle = "Head/tail breaks, Fisher–Jenks and quantiles",
    x = "Conflict index",
    y = "Cumulative proportion",
    fill = "Class"
  )
```

The top three classes of `headtails` contain five observations, whereas those of
`fisher` contain 13. In this example, `headtails` gives more detail at the upper
end of the distribution.

The next plot compares smoothed distributions across methods. For this
comparison, the original `totcon` values are rescaled and rounded to the
same five levels as the class indices.

```{r}
#| label: 20200405_benchmarkbreaks
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Smoothed distributions of class indices for original rescaled values,
#|   head/tail breaks, Fisher–Jenks and quantiles. Head/tail breaks concentrates
#|   observations in the lowest class, while quantiles distributes them
#|   approximately evenly across five classes.

# Rescale values for visualization
afcon$data <- rescale(afcon$totcon,
  to = range(afcon$headtails_br) + c(-0.4, 0.4)
) |> round()

afcon |>
  as_tibble() |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(data, headtails_br, fisher_br, quantile_br),
    names_to = "class_name",
    values_to = "class"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    class_name = case_when(
      class_name %in% c("data", "original") ~ "Original values (rescaled)",
      class_name == "headtails_br" ~ "Head/tail breaks",
      class_name == "fisher_br" ~ "Fisher–Jenks",
      TRUE ~ "Quantiles"
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(class_name = fct_inorder(class_name)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_density(
    aes(x = class, color = class_name),
    key_glyph = draw_key_path,
    trim = TRUE,
    adjust = .75,
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = label_comma(accuracy = 1),
    breaks = seq(1, nclass, 1)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_comma()) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "cividis") +
  labs(
    title = "How the methods distribute observations across classes",
    subtitle = "Smoothed distributions of class indices",
    x = "Rescaled value / Class index",
    y = "Estimated density",
    color = "Classification method"
  )
```

In this example, the class assignments from `headtails` retain more of the
original imbalance. By contrast, `quantile` aims for similar numbers of
observations per class, regardless of the gaps between values.

The maps show where these differences appear. Circle size and color encode
the rescaled conflict index in the unclassified panel and the assigned class
in each of the other three panels.

```{r}
#| label: 20200405_finalplot
#| fig-cap: ""
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig-alt: >-
#|   Four maps of Africa compare the rescaled conflict index with head/tail
#|   breaks, Fisher–Jenks and quantiles. Circle size and color represent the
#|   rescaled index in the first map and the assigned class in the other three.

library(giscoR)
library(sf)

africa <- gisco_get_countries(
  resolution = 60,
  region = "Africa",
  epsg = 3857
) |>
  st_transform("ESRI:102024")

africa_focus <- st_linestring(rbind(
  c(-20, 40),
  c(60, 40),
  c(60, -40),
  c(-20, -40),
  c(-20, 40)
)) |>
  st_segmentize(5) |>
  st_cast("POLYGON") |>
  st_sfc(crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(st_crs(africa)) |>
  st_bbox()

afcon_sf <- st_as_sf(afcon, crs = 4326, coords = c("x", "y")) |>
  st_transform(st_crs(africa)) |>
  arrange(desc(totcon))

afcon_sf |>
  mutate(original = rescale(totcon, to = c(1, 5))) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(original, headtails_br, fisher_br, quantile_br),
    names_to = "class_name",
    values_to = "class"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    class_name = case_when(
      class_name %in% c("data", "original") ~ "Original values (rescaled)",
      class_name == "headtails_br" ~ "Head/tail breaks",
      class_name == "fisher_br" ~ "Fisher–Jenks",
      TRUE ~ "Quantiles"
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(class_name = fct_inorder(class_name)) |>
  arrange(desc(totcon)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = africa, color = "grey80", fill = "grey80") +
  geom_sf(aes(size = class, color = class)) +
  coord_sf(
    xlim = c(africa_focus[c("xmin", "xmax")]),
    ylim = c(africa_focus[c("ymin", "ymax")]),
    expand = FALSE
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~class_name) +
  guides(
    color = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE),
    size = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)
  ) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(
    option = "cividis",
    alpha = 0.75,
    breaks = seq(1, 5, 1)
  ) +
  theme(
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.line = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "How classification changes the map",
    subtitle = "Symbol sizes represent original values or assigned classes",
    color = "Class index",
    size = "Class index"
  )
```

Head/tail breaks separates the highest index values into smaller groups.
Fisher–Jenks spreads the middle and lower values across more classes, which
makes distinctions among countries in West Africa easier to see in this
example. Quantiles keep class sizes similar. The choice depends on which part
of the distribution the map needs to emphasize.

```{r}
#| label: 20200405_og_africa
#| include: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.15
#| dpi: 200
#| fig-crop: true

bbox2 <- st_linestring(rbind(
  c(-20, 25),
  c(60, 25),
  c(60, 0),
  c(-20, 0),
  c(-20, 25)
)) |>
  st_segmentize(5) |>
  st_cast("POLYGON") |>
  st_sfc(crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(st_crs(africa)) |>
  st_bbox()

afcon_sf |>
  arrange(desc(totcon)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = africa, color = "#646464", fill = "#FEFEE9") +
  geom_sf(aes(size = totcon, color = totcon)) +
  coord_sf(
    xlim = c(bbox2[c("xmin", "xmax")]),
    ylim = c(bbox2[c("ymin", "ymax")]),
    expand = FALSE
  ) +
  guides(
    color = "none",
    size = "none"
  ) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 20, min) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(
    direction = -1,
    alpha = 0.75,
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.background = element_blank(),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#C6ECFF"),
    panel.border = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank(),
    axis.line = element_blank(),
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank()
  )
```
